title: API response ladders for common failures (timeouts, 429s, streaming, elevated errors)
body:
Purpose and scope:
This is a lightweight set of response "ladders" and quick probes for the most common API failure modes we run into from production: hard timeouts, client-facing 429s (rate limiting/throttling), degraded streaming throughput/latency, and elevated error rates (5xx spikes).

This is intentionally informal: think "on-call note + triage ladder" that an engineer can use in the first 15 minutes of an incident. Longer-term playbooks (rollbacks, postmortems) live elsewhere.

Quick principles (tl;dr):
- First 5 min: determine scope (routes/customers/regions), surface impact, and set comms (pager channel + incident record).
- Surface telemetry: per-route latency P50/P90/P99, error-rate, 429-rate, streaming chunk durations, worker restarts, and recent deploys.
- Apply cheap mitigations first (traffic shaping, fallback routing, reduced concurrency) before doing risky changes.
- Preserve telemetry for postmortem (don't over-delete logs).

---
Initial checks (0-5 min):
1) Confirm alert and define scope
   - Which alert fired? (SLO, synthetic, customer report)
   - Affected routes / models / tenants / regions? Use Console -> Per-route dashboards and the synthetic checks page.
2) High-level health probes
   - Check control plane: auth, routing (console health status).
   - Check serving runtime: worker pod counts, recent restarts (kubectl get pods --namespace serving -o wide; kubectl describe pod <suspect-pod>), host-level OOM/killing in node events.
   - Check model process metrics (GPU/CPU utilization, memory) via Prometheus/Grafana.
3) Recent changes
   - Any deploys in last 30 minutes? (CI/CD pipeline / GitHub PR list)
   - Any config changes (ratelimit, routing policy, quota updates)?

Timeouts (signature: client sees deadline_exceeded, high p99 latency)
Signature to confirm:
- P99 token-latency/response-latency rising across multiple hosts or specific model workers.
- Increased request queuing (queue_size metrics) and longer request_wait_time.
Possible causes:
- Model-level stalls (OOM, kernel-level slowdown)
- Worker saturation or mis-sized batch windows
- Network blips between frontends and backends
- Backend dependency (KV cache) slow or thrashing
Fast probes and commands:
- Check per-worker queued requests: curl http://serving-metrics:9100/worker/queue or use grafana -> worker queue_size
- kubectl top pods to spot saturation
- dmesg / syslog on impacted nodes for OOM kills
Quick mitigations (low-risk to higher-risk):
1) Reduce client concurrency target (front-end throttle): temporarily lower per-connection concurrency to reduce queuing.
2) Shorten batching window / batch size in runtime config (hot patch config or toggle via feature flag).
3) Route a subset of traffic to dedicated capacity or a fallback model variant.
4) If single-host hotspot: cordon + restart problematic worker (kubectl drain/cordon then restart).
5) If an imminent risk of widespread outages and root cause is model OOM or kernel crash: roll back last deploy or toggle to a smaller model.
Notes to on-call: avoid immediate mass restarts across region (can make queue spike worse). Prefer targeted cordon + restart and gradual traffic rebalancing.

429s and rate-limit spikes (signature: client receives 429; rate of 429s increases sharply)
Signature to confirm:
- Spike in 429_count metric correlated with overall request rate or a specific API key/tenant.
- Rate limiter metrics showing exhausted tokens or full queues.
Possible causes:
- Legit client traffic spikes (legitimate or replay)
- Buggy client retry storms or looped requests
- Misconfigured quota (sudden policy change, staging key hitting prod limits)
- Upstream throttles or circuit-breakers tripping
Fast probes and commands:
- Identify top callers: query logs (sum by api_key / tenant) for 429s in the last 5m.
- Check rate limiter backend: redis or token-bucket metrics (latency, errors, evictions).
- Look for recent policy deploys (feature flags, quota updates).
Quick mitigations:
1) Open a temporary grace window for known heavy tenants (bump quota for specific API key) via admin console.
2) Apply global short-lived ingress backpressure: reduce allowed RPS at the frontend LB.
3) If caused by client retry storms, contact owners and issue temporary bans or stricter backoff headers.
4) If rate limiter storage is unhealthy (Redis latency/evictions), promote a hot-standby or failover to alternate store.
5) If bot/replay traffic, apply IP-based or signature-based filtering at edge.
Notes and gotchas:
- Be conservative with global quota increases; prefer per-tenant exceptions to avoid exhausting capacity.
- Preserve request logs for 30–90 minutes for debugging.

Degraded streaming (signature: streaming responses are choppy, long inter-chunk delays, or client sees intermittent EOF)
Signature to confirm:
- Chunk latency (time between stream chunks) increases and jitter spikes.
- Worker CPU/async-loop stalls visible in tracer (span durations grow)
Possible causes:
- Backpressure on generator thread (KV cache misses, slow model forward passes for long contexts)
- Network packet drops or TLS handshake latency between nodes
- Resource contention: too many concurrent streams on a worker (event-loop saturation)
Fast probes and commands:
- Query stream chunk latency histogram in grafana for the route.
- Check connection counts per worker and max-open-streams metric.
- tcpdump of a single affected connection if network suspected.
Quick mitigations:
1) Move long-running streaming sessions to dedicated streaming pool (route by header)
2) Temporarily bump worker pool size for streaming heavy routes
3) Reduce server-side max_chunk_size or switch to non-streaming fallback for new requests to reduce head-of-line blocking
4) Enable KV cache priming for the top N prefixes if repeated prefixes cause misses
5) If it's a network issue, failover traffic to another region or AZ (if acceptable latency tradeoff)
Notes:
- Avoid killing all streaming workers at once; restart single worker and observe impact.
- Streaming problems often look like timeouts + 5xx symptoms mixed — check both ladders.

Elevated error rates (5xx spikes) (signature: error-rate climbs, 502/503/500 predominates)
Signature to confirm:
- Check error-class distribution (model OOM vs kernel panic vs dependency 502).
- Correlate with worker restarts, pod OOMs, node-level errors, and infra changes.
Possible causes:
- Downstream dependency failing (model cache, feature store, auth service)
- Deployment with breaking change or bad config
- Resource exhaustion (disk, memory, ephemeral port exhaustion)
Fast probes and commands:
- Check logs for error class frequency: grep "ERROR" /var/log/serving/... or use centralized logging filters
- kubectl get events, describe pods to surface OOMKilled containers
- Check recent scaling actions (autoscaler events)
Quick mitigations:
1) Disable the failing dependency via feature flag or fall back to cached responses if present
2) Temporarily limit write-heavy requests to reduce load and give dependency breathing room
3) Rollback recent deploy if strong signal that change caused the spike
4) If model process is OOMing, reduce model instance size or switch to a smaller quantized variant
5) If network or infra is unhealthy, fail traffic to alternate region or engage infra to remediate nodes
Notes:
- Preserve a sample of failing request traces (not all) for postmortem; tag traces with incident id.

Escalation and communication ladder
- 0–10m: On-call signals the incident in #sre-incident, creates the incident document (link in header), and pings the rotation manager if > 15m without progress.
- 15–30m: If mitigations don't regain SLO coverage, escalate to on-call SRE TL and product manager for affected product line.
- 30–60m: If customer impact is large (multiple enterprise tenants), involve account owners/CS and engineer a customer-facing update (status page update).
- >60m: Consider paged exec and leadership if no progress or outages expanding.

Post-incident hooks (short list to attach to incident):
- Capture topology and sequence-of-events (timestamps) + the first-alert graphs.
- Save all relevant traces and sample logs (min 30 minutes pre and post) and attach to the incident.
- TODOs for next 72 hours: followup experiments (e.g., add histograms for batch waiting time, better per-tenant quota visibility, streaming queue metrics).

Runbook TODOs and open questions (notes to self):
- Add a pre-baked incident dashboard for this ladder (P90, P99, queue_size, restarts, 429_rate, chunk_latency) — currently partial.
- Investigate an automated circuit-breaker that triggers a safe fallback model when p99 latency crosses threshold for 2 consecutive windows.
- Define a safe per-tenant temporary quota increase process (audit trail + TTL) so SREs can act faster without billing risk.
- Add playbook for multi-region failover for streaming (need more testing for TLS session migration).

Appendix: quick command cheatsheet
- kubectl get pods -n serving | sort -k3
- kubectl describe pod <pod> -n serving
- kubectl logs <pod> -n serving --since=15m | grep -i "error" | wc -l
- curl "https://console.redwood/api/metrics/route?route=chat-generate&window=5m"
- jq and sed snippets for filtering logs: cat logs.json | jq '.entries[] | select(.status==429) | {api_key: .meta.key, ts: .ts}'

Contact list and rotations
- SRE on-call (primary): oncall-sre@redwood.com (see internal rota)
- SRE TL: eng-sre-tl@redwood.com
- Platform infra pager: infra-pager@redwood.com

Keep this doc lean and update with any new learnings. If you test a mitigation that helps, add the exact steps and timestamps into the incident log so we can codify safer automation later.
